Well, they come and go, I suppose. It's not every single second of the day, but it happens enough that I finally came in to see somebody about it. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, they do. It's gotten really bad, actually. I got to the point where my aide job was in danger because I was missing shifts and mixing up my care notes. I just couldn't keep my visits organized the way I used to, you know? It's like my brain was a scrambled egg. 

I used to be so organized. I had this beautiful planner I bought at the stationery store downtown. The one with the green awning? They have the loveliest paper there, thick and creamy, and those pens that just glide when you write. I always used a blue pen for Mrs. Higgins and a red one for Mr. Henderson's schedule. Red is such a powerful color. I had a red coat once, a real wool peacoat I got at a thrift store. It was missing a button, but I found a replacement that almost matched. I wore it everywhere until the lining started to tear. I tried to fix it with that handheld sewing machine, but you know how that went. It just made a mess of the silk. Silk is so delicate. You have to wash it by hand in the sink with baby shampoo. Did you know that? Baby shampoo is so gentle. It smells like powder and... well, babies, I guess. 

But yes, the voices made everything so hard. I even stopped going to my walking club on Tuesday mornings, and I haven't been to the library art talks in weeks. I love those art talks. Last time we learned about water lilies, the ones Monet painted. He had cataracts, you know, which is why his later paintings are so blurry and red. My aunt had cataracts, and she refused to get the surgery. She just sat in the dark watching game shows. I didn't want to end up like that, but I just found myself mostly alone at home, listening to those voices judging me instead of going out.

Well, yes, absolutely. It's like... my thoughts run so fast, just racing all the time. One minute I'm thinking about making sure I have a client's medicine right, and then suddenly I'm worrying about how I'm going to pay rent, and then my mind jumps to the title of a painting I saw once, and then I'm fixated on some secret message in a song playing on the radio. I just can't slow it down enough to make sense of anything. 

It reminds me of this radio I used to have, a little silver transistor one with a long antenna. I'd carry it around the house when I was doing my chores. I loved listening to the oldies station. They played a lot of Motown. My favorite was always The Supremes. Diana Ross had such gorgeous dresses, didn't she? All those sequins catching the light. No, I wouldn't say that. Things feel very real to me. Sometimes too real, you know? Like everything is just pressing in so hard. But no, not like a dream.

Well, yes, I suppose I do have those times. It's like... sometimes I feel just so incredibly bright and full of energy, like I've been chosen for something important, and all of Greenville just isn't big enough to hold all the plans I have in my head. But then, almost out of nowhere, I get so irritable. I'll snap hard at someone over the smallest thing, like if one of my clients just asks me to repeat myself. 

I had this one client, Mr. Abernathy, he was always asking me to repeat myself. He refused to wear his hearing aids. He said they whistled too much. I told him he just needed to get them adjusted at the audiologist, but he was stubborn. He was a retired train conductor, you know. He had this whole room in his basement dedicated to model trains. It was incredible, really. He had little mountains made of paper mache, and tiny trees, and a little town with a diner and a post office. The post office even had a tiny American flag on a flagpole made from a toothpick. I used to buy those fancy toothpicks, the ones with the little frilly cellophane at the end, for when I made club sandwiches. A good club sandwich needs three slices of bread, toasted just right. If you don't toast it, the bread gets soggy from the tomatoes. I grow my own tomatoes in the summer, big beefsteak ones. The squirrels always try to get them before they're ripe, though. I tried putting up a plastic owl to scare them away, but one day I looked out the window and a squirrel was sitting right on top of the owl's head, eating an acorn. They're so brazen, those squirrels. 

But yes, going from feeling so grand and full of plans to just snapping at people... it happens, and it lasts for a while when it does.

Well, yes, I suppose I do. It's just that my thoughts run so fast, you know? Like, one minute I'm thinking about whether I gave Mrs. Higgins her afternoon medicine, and then suddenly I'm worrying about how I'm going to pay the rent this month, and then I'm trying to remember the title of that painting I saw at the library, and then I'm thinking about a message hidden in a song I heard on the radio... it's just all happening at once. The keys were so sticky anyway, probably from kids eating candy while they played those educational games. I never liked candy much, except for those little strawberry candies wrapped in foil that looks like a strawberry? My neighbor Mrs. Gable always kept a glass dish of them on her front hall table. She had a beautiful hall table, real mahogany with claw feet. \n\nBut yes, my thoughts just go and go. We got our honey from this local farmer down the road, Mr. Henderson. He had these white boxes stacked up in his field for the bees. He always wore that funny suit with the net over his face. I've always been terrified of bees ever since I got stung on the eyelid when I was seven. It swelled up completely shut for three days. My teacher, Mrs. Albright, thought I had pink eye and sent me to the nurse. The nurse's office always smelled like rubbing alcohol and those little paper cups. \n\nBut no, things around me feel real. I bought it at a yard sale for two dollars. The woman selling it was moving to Florida, she said. Florida seems too hot to me. The water was always too warm, like bathwater. I don't like warm pools, it feels unnatural. Like you're swimming in a giant bathtub with strangers. It's almost too nice to throw away, so I just keep stacking them up in the drawer.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely irritable, anxious, or depressed that lasted for more than a few days?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I do have those times. I tried putting up a plastic owl to scare them away, but one day I looked out the window and a squirrel was sitting right on top of the owl's head, eating an acorn. They're so brazen, those squirrels. \n\nBut yes, going from feeling so grand and full of plans to just snapping at people... it happens, and it lasts for a while when it does.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself jumping from one topic to another when speaking, without really finishing your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I do. Well, yes, I definitely have those times. It's like a switch flips and I just have so much energy, I can't even sit down. I'll stay up all night and just do everything at once. Well, yes, I suppose I have. When I'm not all wound up with that crazy energy, I just... I don't care about any of it anymore. I can sit at the kitchen table for hours, just staring, with my coffee getting completely cold. I used to love painting water colors. The way the colors bleed into each other on the thick paper, it's almost like magic. You have to use a special kind of paper, cold-pressed, otherwise it just buckles and ruins the whole picture. I bought a whole pad of it on sale at the craft store once. My neighbor's dog howls every time the bus goes by. It's a beagle, I think. They have such floppy ears.

I just can't slow it down enough to make sense of anything. \n\nIt reminds me of this radio I used to have, a little silver transistor one with a long antenna. I'd carry it around the house when I was doing my chores. I loved listening to the oldies station. They played a lot of Motown. My favorite was always The Supremes. I never liked candy much, except for those little strawberry candies wrapped in foil that looks like a strawberry? My neighbor Mrs. Gable always kept a glass dish of them on her front hall table. She had a beautiful hall table, real mahogany with claw feet. \n\nBut yes, my thoughts just go and go. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Well, yes, my sleep gets completely turned upside down. I've gone so many nights where I'll lay down for maybe two or three hours, tops, and then I just pop right out of bed feeling completely charged up, like I slept for ten hours. I'll get right back up and start painting again, or I'll start making phone calls to people, even though it's the middle of the night. 

I called my sister once at 3 AM because I had this brilliant idea for a new way to organize her pantry. She wasn't very happy about that. She lives in Florida now, right near the beach. I've always wanted to live near the ocean. The sound of the waves crashing is supposed to be very soothing, like a white noise machine. I bought one of those machines once, but it just sounded like static on a TV. Do you remember when TVs used to have actual static when the station went off the air? Now they just go to a blue screen. Blue is a calming color, they say. That's why hospitals use so much light blue. My bedroom used to be painted light blue, but then I decided it was too cold, so I painted it yellow. Yellow is supposed to be cheerful, like a sunflower. Sunflowers grow so tall, they look like they're trying to touch the sun. I wonder if they ever get sunburned. Probably not, since they're plants. 

But yes, I just don't sleep much at all during those times. Two or three hours and I'm up, making calls and painting like I never even went to bed.

Like I said, I came in because I keep hearing them, clear as somebody standing right there in my little studio with me, even when the house is totally quiet and nobody is there. It's just so strange, isn't it? \n\nSpeaking of quiet, Mrs. Higgins—she's one of my clients, I help her with her meals and things—she has this clock in her living room that ticks so loudly. Tick, tick, tick, all day long. It's one of those grandfather clocks, beautiful dark wood, maybe mahogany? I read somewhere that mahogany is getting harder to find because they're cutting down all the rainforests. It's a shame, really. All those poor monkeys losing their homes. I saw a documentary about monkeys once, the ones with the long tails that swing from the branches. They looked like they were having so much fun. I always wanted to go to the jungle, but the bugs would probably eat me alive. Mosquitoes love me. I can't even sit on my own porch in the summer without getting covered in bites. I tried those citronella candles, but they smell like a lemon went bad. My neighbor, Mr. Henderson, he planted some kind of special bush that's supposed to keep bugs away, but his dog keeps digging it up. Poor Mr. Henderson, he tries so hard with his garden. \n\nBut no, the voices don't really sound like my own thoughts, they just keep telling me my work is being judged.\n\nDoctor: Do these voices and the feeling of being judged cause you a lot of distress or interfere with your daily life?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, they do. It's gotten really bad, actually. I got to the point where my aide job was in danger because I was missing shifts and mixing up my care notes. I just couldn't keep my visits organized the way I used to, you know? It's like my brain was a scrambled egg. \n\nI used to be so organized. I had this beautiful planner I bought at the stationery store downtown. The one with the green awning? They have the loveliest paper there, thick and creamy, and those pens that just glide when you write. I always used a blue pen for Mrs. Higgins and a red one for Mr. Henderson's schedule. Red is such a powerful color. I had a red coat once, a real wool peacoat I got at a thrift store. It was missing a button, but I found a replacement that almost matched. I wore it everywhere until the lining started to tear. I tried to fix it with that handheld sewing machine, but you know how that went. It just made a mess of the silk. Silk is so delicate. You have to wash it by hand in the sink with baby shampoo. Did you know that? Baby shampoo is so gentle. It smells like powder and... well, babies, I guess. \n\nBut yes, the voices made everything so hard. I even stopped going to my walking club on Tuesday mornings, and I haven't been to the library art talks in weeks. I love those art talks. Last time we learned about water lilies, the ones Monet painted. He had cataracts, you know, which is why his later paintings are so blurry and red. My aunt had cataracts, and she refused to get the surgery. She just sat in the dark watching game shows. I didn't want to end up like that, but I just found myself mostly alone at home, listening to those voices judging me instead of going out.\n\nDoctor: Do you think the voices are coming from something or someone that is actually outside of you, or are they just in your mind?\n\nPatient: Well, like I keep saying, I know they're outside of me because they sound just as clear as somebody standing right there in my little studio. It's not just in my head. I hear them saying my name, telling me my work is being judged, even when the house is completely quiet and I know for a fact nobody else is there. I always keep the deadbolt locked, you know. You just can't be too careful with people wandering around these days. \n\nMy mailman, Jim, he was telling me about some stolen packages over on Elm Street. Jim is such a sweetheart, he always walks my mail right up to the porch steps because he knows I worry. He has a terrible limp, though, especially when it rains. His knee acts up. My uncle had a bad knee from his days working at the lumber mill, and he used to rub this awful green ointment on it. It smelled like peppermint and gasoline. He kept it in this little metal tin on the coffee table. I used to love collecting tins when I was younger. Mostly those butter cookie tins they sell around Christmas? The ones you open thinking there are cookies inside, but it's always just somebody's sewing supplies. My grandmother kept her buttons in one. She had thousands of buttons. Pearl ones, brass ones, little plastic ones shaped like anchors. I swallowed a button once when I was four, and my mother panicked and called the ambulance. The siren was so loud, it made the neighbor's dogs howl for an hour. \n\nBut yes, the voices. They aren't my mind playing tricks. They are right there in the room with me, clear as day, even when I'm totally alone.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced any particularly stressful or traumatic events in the last year or so?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose. This whole thing, it's been going on for about a year and five months now. It all started right around the time my work hours got cut at the agency, and my money situation got so much worse. It was terribly stressful, trying to figure out how to pay the electric bill. \n\nElectricity is so expensive now, isn't it? I remember when I was a girl, we had this little space heater that we'd plug in during the winter, the kind with the glowing orange coils. You could see the dust burning off it if you looked close enough. My brother, Tommy, he used to try and toast marshmallows on it, which was a terrible idea. He got gooey marshmallow all over the carpet, and my mother was absolutely furious. She spent hours scrubbing it with a toothbrush and some kind of harsh soap. She had the most beautiful hands, my mother, always wearing those yellow rubber gloves when she cleaned. I tried to buy some of those gloves last week at the pharmacy, but they only had the purple ones. Purple is such a strange color for cleaning, don't you think? It makes me think of eggplants, and I've never liked eggplants. They're too squishy when you cook them. \n\nBut yes, the stress. About a year and five months ago, when they cut my hours and the money got so tight. That's when it all started.\n\nDoctor: Do you ever find it hard to stay on topic or keep your thoughts straight when talking to someone?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, absolutely. It's like... my thoughts run so fast, just racing all the time. One minute I'm thinking about making sure I have a client's medicine right, and then suddenly I'm worrying about how I'm going to pay rent, and then my mind jumps to the title of a painting I saw once, and then I'm fixated on some secret message in a song playing on the radio. I just can't slow it down enough to make sense of anything. \n\nIt reminds me of this radio I used to have, a little silver transistor one with a long antenna. I'd carry it around the house when I was doing my chores. I loved listening to the oldies station. They played a lot of Motown. My favorite was always The Supremes. Diana Ross had such gorgeous dresses, didn't she? All those sequins catching the light. I tried to sew sequins onto a denim jacket once, but it took forever. The needle kept getting stuck, and I pricked my finger so many times I had to put band-aids on all my fingertips. It made typing on the computer at the library impossible. The keys were so sticky anyway, probably from kids eating candy while they played those educational games. I never liked candy much, except for those little strawberry candies wrapped in foil that looks like a strawberry? My neighbor Mrs. Gable always kept a glass dish of them on her front hall table. She had a beautiful hall table, real mahogany with claw feet. \n\nBut yes, my thoughts just go and go. From the medicine to the rent to the painting to the song... it's just so fast, I can't keep them straight at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you're living in a dream or that things around you aren't real?\n\nPatient: No, I wouldn't say that. Things feel very real to me. Sometimes too real, you know? Like everything is just pressing in so hard. But no, not like a dream. \n\nI used to have the most vivid dreams, though, especially when I was pregnant with my daughter. They say pregnancy hormones do that to you. I dreamt once that I was swimming in a giant bowl of tomato soup, and the croutons were the size of rowboats. I woke up craving grilled cheese so badly. We used to make grilled cheese in this heavy cast-iron skillet my grandmother gave me. It weighed a ton, you needed two hands just to lift it off the stove. She used it for everything—frying chicken, making cornbread. Her cornbread was always a little dry, to be honest, but we never told her. We'd just drown it in butter and honey. We got our honey from this local farmer down the road, Mr. Henderson. He had these white boxes stacked up in his field for the bees. He always wore that funny suit with the net over his face. I've always been terrified of bees ever since I got stung on the eyelid when I was seven. It swelled up completely shut for three days. My teacher, Mrs. Albright, thought I had pink eye and sent me to the nurse. The nurse's office always smelled like rubbing alcohol and those little paper cups. \n\nBut no, things around me feel real. It doesn't feel like a dream at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt like you've lost touch with reality or had a breakdown in your ability to function normally?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, things really fell apart for me day-to-day. I got to the point where my job as an aide was in serious danger. I was missing my shifts, and I kept mixing up all my care notes. I just couldn't keep my client visits organized the way I used to at all. \n\nI used to be so organized, you know. I had this special leather binder for my notes, a beautiful burgundy color. I bought it at a yard sale for two dollars. The woman selling it was moving to Florida, she said. Florida seems too hot to me. I went to Orlando once in August and I thought I was going to melt right into the pavement. We stayed at this motel that had a pool shaped like a guitar. The water was always too warm, like bathwater. I don't like warm pools, it feels unnatural. Like you're swimming in a giant bathtub with strangers. The chlorine smell took days to wash out of my favorite swimsuit. It was a one-piece with little white polka dots. Polka dots are so cheerful, don't you think? Minnie Mouse always wore polka dots. \n\nBut yes, my functioning... it wasn't just work that fell apart. I completely stopped going to my walking club. And I used to go to these wonderful art talks at the library, but I stopped going to those too. So I just ended up being mostly alone at home all the time. \n\nMy house gets so quiet when I'm alone. And drafty, especially near the front door. I bought one of those draft dodgers, the kind that looks like a long dachshund dog, to put at the bottom of the door. It has little button eyes. One of the buttons is loose, and I keep meaning to sew it back on tight, but I can never find my sewing kit. I think I left it in the kitchen drawer with the takeout menus. We have this new Chinese place that opened up, and their menus are printed on this really thick, glossy paper. It's almost too nice to throw away, so I just keep stacking them up in the drawer.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely irritable, anxious, or depressed that lasted for more than a few days?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I do have those times. It's like... sometimes I feel just so incredibly bright and full of energy, like I've been chosen for something important, and all of Greenville just isn't big enough to hold all the plans I have in my head. But then, almost out of nowhere, I get so irritable. I'll snap hard at someone over the smallest thing, like if one of my clients just asks me to repeat myself. \n\nI had this one client, Mr. Abernathy, he was always asking me to repeat myself. He refused to wear his hearing aids. He said they whistled too much. I told him he just needed to get them adjusted at the audiologist, but he was stubborn. He was a retired train conductor, you know. He had this whole room in his basement dedicated to model trains. It was incredible, really. He had little mountains made of paper mache, and tiny trees, and a little town with a diner and a post office. The post office even had a tiny American flag on a flagpole made from a toothpick. I used to buy those fancy toothpicks, the ones with the little frilly cellophane at the end, for when I made club sandwiches. A good club sandwich needs three slices of bread, toasted just right. If you don't toast it, the bread gets soggy from the tomatoes. I grow my own tomatoes in the summer, big beefsteak ones. The squirrels always try to get them before they're ripe, though. I tried putting up a plastic owl to scare them away, but one day I looked out the window and a squirrel was sitting right on top of the owl's head, eating an acorn. They're so brazen, those squirrels. \n\nBut yes, going from feeling so grand and full of plans to just snapping at people... it happens, and it lasts for a while when it does.\n\nDoctor: Do you often find yourself jumping from one topic to another when speaking, without really finishing your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I do. It's just that my thoughts run so fast, you know? Like, one minute I'm thinking about whether I gave Mrs. Higgins her afternoon medicine, and then suddenly I'm worrying about how I'm going to pay the rent this month, and then I'm trying to remember the title of that painting I saw at the library, and then I'm thinking about a message hidden in a song I heard on the radio... it's just all happening at once. I can't slow it down enough to make sense of it sometimes. \n\nThe radio in my car only gets AM stations now. The dial broke off last winter when it was so freezing cold. I had these thick wool mittens on, the kind with the fleece lining inside, and I just snapped the knob right off trying to turn down the volume. Those mittens were a gift from my sister, Claire. She lives out in Oregon now, where it rains all the time. She says the rain is good for her garden, but I think it would just make everything muddy. I hate tracking mud into the house. I have this beautiful braided rug in my entryway, it's all different shades of blue and gray. I bought it at a craft fair from a woman who spins her own yarn. She had this big wooden spinning wheel right there in her booth, just pumping the pedal with her foot like something out of a fairy tale. Fairy tales always have spinning wheels in them, don't they? Like Sleeping Beauty. I always thought it was silly that a whole kingdom fell asleep just because one girl pricked her finger. \n\nBut yes, my thoughts just race from one thing to the next, medicine, rent, paintings, songs... it's exhausting trying to keep up with my own head.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever had a period where you felt extremely energetic or unusually happy for more than a few days?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I definitely have those times. It's like a switch flips and I just have so much energy, I can't even sit down. I'll stay up all night and just do everything at once. I'll clean the whole kitchen from top to bottom, start three different paintings, crochet half a blanket, and rewrite all my care schedules before the sun even comes up. \n\nI learned to crochet from my grandmother. She used to make these beautiful afghans, all zig-zags of pink and brown. Brown is such an underappreciated color, I think. It's so earthy and grounding. Like the soil in my garden after a good rain. I tried growing zucchini last year, but they just took over the whole plot. Zucchini is funny that way, you turn your back for a second and suddenly you have squashes the size of baseball bats. I tried making zucchini bread, but I left it in the oven too long and the edges got all hard and crusty. I had to throw the whole loaf out for the birds. The birds in my yard are mostly just sparrows and starlings, nothing very colorful. I'd love to see a cardinal, they're so bright red. Red is a power color, you know. That's why politicians always wear red ties. \n\nBut yes, that energy... it's just so much all at once, cleaning and painting and crocheting, just going and going without stopping.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed a significant decline in your ability to perform daily tasks or maintain relationships over the past year?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I have. It got to the point where my job as an aide was really in danger. I was missing shifts, and I'd mix up the care notes for my clients. I just couldn't keep the visits organized the way I used to, you know? It was all just slipping away from me. \n\nI used to be so organized, too. I had this big planner, the kind with the leather cover and the little ribbon to mark your page. I always bought the ones with the weekly view, not the daily view, because the daily view just feels too overwhelming. Too many lines on one page. Lines remind me of lined paper from school. I never did finish high school, you know. I left in the 11th grade. Sometimes I think about going back for my GED, but then I remember how much I hated algebra. Who really needs to know how to find 'x' anyway? Unless you're a pirate looking for buried treasure. I saw a movie about pirates once, they had these huge ships with enormous white sails. I wonder how they kept those sails so clean out on the ocean. Maybe the salt water acts like a natural bleach. I use vinegar to clean my windows at home, it works better than the blue stuff you buy at the store. The blue stuff always leaves streaks. \n\nBut yes, my job was really suffering. And I stopped going to my walking club, too, and those art talks I loved at the library. I just ended up mostly alone at home all the time, not doing much of anything at all.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in how much you enjoy the things you used to like doing?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, I suppose I have. When I'm not all wound up with that crazy energy, I just... I don't care about any of it anymore. I can sit at the kitchen table for hours, just staring, with my coffee getting completely cold. I don't answer the phone when it rings, I don't go to the walking club like I mentioned, and I don't even care to pick up my paintbrush. \n\nI used to love painting water colors. The way the colors bleed into each other on the thick paper, it's almost like magic. You have to use a special kind of paper, cold-pressed, otherwise it just buckles and ruins the whole picture. I bought a whole pad of it on sale at the craft store once. The cashier there had the most interesting hair, it was dyed bright purple, like an eggplant. I've always wondered what it would be like to have purple hair. Maybe people would take me more seriously, or maybe they'd just stare. People stare a lot anyway, especially when you're waiting for the bus. The bus system here is just terrible. You wait for an hour and then three show up all at once, right in a row. It makes no sense. The buses are always so loud, too, with those squeaky brakes. My neighbor's dog howls every time the bus goes by. It's a beagle, I think. They have such floppy ears. \n\nBut yes, I just lose all interest. The coffee gets cold, the phone rings, the paintbrushes sit there... I just don't have the care to do any of it.\n\nDoctor: Have you noticed any changes in your sleep patterns over the past year?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, my sleep gets completely turned upside down. I've gone so many nights where I'll lay down for maybe two or three hours, tops, and then I just pop right out of bed feeling completely charged up, like I slept for ten hours. I'll get right back up and start painting again, or I'll start making phone calls to people, even though it's the middle of the night. \n\nI called my sister once at 3 AM because I had this brilliant idea for a new way to organize her pantry. She wasn't very happy about that. She lives in Florida now, right near the beach. I've always wanted to live near the ocean. The sound of the waves crashing is supposed to be very soothing, like a white noise machine. I bought one of those machines once, but it just sounded like static on a TV. Do you remember when TVs used to have actual static when the station went off the air? Now they just go to a blue screen. Blue is a calming color, they say. That's why hospitals use so much light blue. My bedroom used to be painted light blue, but then I decided it was too cold, so I painted it yellow. Yellow is supposed to be cheerful, like a sunflower. Sunflowers grow so tall, they look like they're trying to touch the sun. I wonder if they ever get sunburned. Probably not, since they're plants. \n\nBut yes, I just don't sleep much at all during those times. Two or three hours and I'm up, making calls and painting like I never even went to bed.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen, smelled, tasted, or felt things that weren't really there?\n\nPatient: Well, yes, actually, that's a big part of why I came in. I keep hearing these voices, clear as day, just like somebody is standing right there in my little studio with me. They say my name, and they tell me my work is being judged. It happens even when the house is completely quiet and I know for a fact nobody else is there. \n\nIt's so strange when the house gets that quiet. You start to hear the refrigerator humming, and the pipes settling. Old houses make the strangest noises. My house was built in the 1940s, I think. Back then, they used real plaster for the walls, not that cheap drywall stuff they use now. Plaster is so much harder to hang a picture on, you have to use a special drill bit or it just crumbles everywhere. I tried to hang a mirror in the hallway once and made a huge mess. It was one of those ornate mirrors with the gold frames. I found it at a flea market. Flea markets are fascinating, you never know what you're going to find. Some people just sell absolute junk, but sometimes you find a real treasure. I saw a man selling antique pocket watches once. They were so intricate, with all those tiny little gears inside. I wonder how anyone has the patience to put those together. You'd need a magnifying glass and tweezers just to see what you were doing. \n\nBut yes, the voices are just so clear. Right there in the studio, telling me I'm being judged, even when I'm completely alone."
